# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Review of "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem" (Varga & Holm comment)

The re-analysis in sections 1–4 is valuable. It uses the Halden microdata to check, and largely confirm, problems that could only be suspected from the working paper:
- non-random attrition;
- the manager-reported output index sitting above organisations' own records;
- the scheduled-hours denominator;
- the nominal revenue comparison.

The conclusion is a different matter. The claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" is not supported by the paper's own numbers, and it contradicts the randomised evidence the authors themselves call the most reliable.

## Arithmetic checks

Most figures reconcile:

| Check | Calculation | Reported |
|---|---|---|
| Manager vs records gap | 98.9 − 95.1 | −3.8 points |
| Actual hours, 27 organisations | 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 | −14.1% |
| Actual hours, 17 organisations | 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 | −13.9% |
| Gain, records + scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Gain, manager index + actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Gain, records + actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 | +10.8% |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 | −2.6% |
| Manager above records in 19 of 23 | sign test, one-sided p ≈ 0.001 | systematic, as claimed |

Two figures do not reconcile.

**1. The hours decomposition in §3 doesn't add up.** Compare the components with the reported total:
- **Components:** 32 scheduled hours + 4 days × 0.7 extra hours + 1.6 hours on the day off = 36.4 hours/week.
- **Reported:** 34.6 hours/week.

The 1.8-hour gap is unexplained. The extra time per day would have to be about 0.25 hours, not 0.7, for the total to hold. Alternatively, the components may be measured on a different base or subset.

**2. The novelty extrapolation in §6 is off.** Energy fell from 0.61 SD to 0.29 SD between months 3 and 6, a drop of about 0.107 SD per month. Continuing in a straight line, it reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." This is minor next to the problem with the extrapolation itself, covered in section 4 below.

## 1. Attrition is listed as corrected, but it isn't

The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems brings the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours; attrition is not adjusted for anywhere.

The attrition finding still matters. Seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the schedule began, which contradicts the working paper's account. That is an important correction to the record.

However, its effect on the estimate is asserted, not measured. Seven organisations ran the reduced schedule for one or two months, so the microdata may include their early output indices. The authors could then:
- compute an intention-to-treat estimate across all 70 organisations, or
- report bounds, such as worst-case imputation or Lee bounds.

As written, attrition is used to support the conclusion without being quantified.

## 2. Table 2 mixes the effect of corrections with changes in sample

Each row of Table 2 uses a different subset: 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. The drop from 23.4% to 10.8% therefore combines two things:
- the corrections themselves;
- the change in which organisations are included.

The Data Note says these subsets are not random and the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The abstract and conclusion still present 10.8% as the result of correcting the 23.4%.

The fix is simple: compute all four specifications on the same 17 organisations, and report their sector mix. Organisations with time-tracking software are plausibly concentrated in professional services and IT.

## 3. One of the record-based measures is itself an hours measure

"Billable hours delivered" is listed among the record-based output measures. For a professional-services firm that cuts hours, billable hours fall almost automatically. That is a reduction in input, not a measured fall in output.

If billable-hour organisations make up a meaningful share of the 23, the record-based index is biased downward. Part of the 3.8-point gap would then come from using hours as an output measure, not from managers rounding toward success. The authors should report the gap separately for billable-hour organisations and for the rest.

## 4. The novelty argument is the weakest step, and the conclusion rests on it

- **The data cannot support the extrapolation.** Two survey points cannot show that energy falls in a straight line to zero. The fall from 0.61 to 0.29 SD fits equally well with energy levelling off at a lasting positive value.
- **Energy is not productivity.** The argument assumes the per-hour output gain tracks self-reported energy, but this is never tested.
- **A direct test was available.** Halden collected the output index *monthly*. If the gain is a novelty effect, output per hour should decline from month 1 to month 6, and the microdata can check this. Using the energy trend as a stand-in when the outcome itself was available is a significant omission.
- **The burden-of-proof argument works against the conclusion.** "The burden of proof lies with those claiming [a durable effect]" justifies saying that durability is not established. It does not justify concluding the effect is zero.

## 5. The conclusion contradicts the paper's own evidence

The paper reports several findings that point the other way:
- **The corrected Halden estimate is still well above zero.** It is +10.8%, and that is before any adjustment for novelty, which the paper does not actually measure.
- **Varden's case-processing result.** The authors call Varden's counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature." The same trial's case-processing stratum meets nearly all of the design standards the comment recommends:
  - randomised, with a concurrent control group;
  - record-based output;
  - actual hours from timesheets;
  - nine months of follow-up.

  It found output per actual hour up 12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4), with output per employee unchanged. Measurement error and selection, two of the three named explanations, cannot account for that result. Only novelty remains, and nine months is a longer test than Halden's six. The comment cites the half of Varden that supports its view and ignores the other half.
- **The estimates converge.** The corrected Halden subset (+10.8%) and Varden's case-processing stratum (+12.5%) agree closely despite very different designs. That points towards a real, moderate effect in work not tied to presence, rather than an artifact.

The abstract also contradicts itself. It says the four problems "account for most of the reported gain" and then that the gains are "entirely an artifact." "Most" is supported; "entirely" is not.

The scope is also stretched. The analysis covers one pilot, but the conclusion is about "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" in general.

A defensible conclusion would read something like this: correcting for measurement roughly halves the Halden estimate; the remaining gain of about 11% is consistent with Varden's randomised case-processing result; whether it lasts is unknown; and in coverage-bound work, output per employee falls.

## 6. The criticism of the meetings analysis misdescribes Varden

The comment calls Varden's meetings analysis "a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup… selected for analysis after the results were known." Varden's paper says otherwise:
- **Data collection:** the meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed.
- **Sample:** the seven offices are *all* the treated case-processing offices, not a selected subgroup.
- **Caveats:** Varden labelled the analysis unregistered and exploratory, said that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism," and registered a confirmatory test.

The fair criticism is narrower:
- the sample is small, with r = 0.71 on n = 7, p ≈ 0.07;
- the meeting data have no pre-period;
- the finding should not be cited as an established mechanism until it is confirmed.

Varden's authors already say the last of these. Note also that if the meetings mechanism holds, it is a real efficiency gain, which counts against "entirely an artifact."

## 7. Smaller points

- **Revenue.** The correction is right, and it matches a concern in my review of the original paper. CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue, though; sector output prices would be better. Revenue also has no bearing on per-hour productivity, so it should not be listed among the problems "accounting for" the gain.
- **Retail.** The −11.2% record-based figure rests on three organisations. It is consistent with Varden's counter stratum, but it should be presented as illustrative.
- **Recommendations.** The §8 recommendations are sound: record-based output, actual hours, a comparison group, at least 18 months of follow-up, and intention-to-treat analysis. They describe a design close to Varden's, which is one more reason Varden's case-processing result needs to be addressed.

## Across the three documents

All three pieces agree on the following:
- Halden's headline +23% is inflated by the scheduled-hours denominator and manager reporting.
- Its claim that the model works in every sector does not hold.
- Coverage-bound work loses output per employee.

What remains open is the size and durability of the per-hour gain in work not tied to presence. Current estimates put it at around 10–13% over six to nine months. Varden's 24-month follow-up and a month-by-month re-analysis of the Halden microdata are the most direct ways to settle it.
